title: Delirium and agitation
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Recognise an acute behavioural change as a trigger to assess immediate physiological and neurological safety, not to assume a confirmed delirium diagnosis.
Use verbal and non-verbal de-escalation and reorientation before any medicine is considered.
Recognise that diagnosis and medicines are for the responsible clinicians.
Distinguish ICU-specific evidence uncertainty about antipsychotics from NICE's limited use in selected distressed hospital patients.

sources.use: NICE CG103 (updated January 2023): recommendations on recognising, preventing, assessing and initially managing delirium
FDA haloperidol label: QT and cardiovascular warnings

SCCM 2018 PADIS and 2025 focused update official recommendation webpages read (not full publications); ICU delirium drug uncertainty and rehabilitation statements only; source reuse permission restricted.
SCCM 2025 official focused recommendation page: conditional sedation preference, uncertain antipsychotic treatment evidence, rehabilitation
Vanderbilt CIBS official clinical-use and permission statement, accessed 24 November 2026; not commercial redistribution permission

required_sources: Full critical-care delirium evidence review (SCCM 2018/2025 PADIS full publications and 2026 national updates) and unit's validated delirium tool protocol
Verify ICDSC rights and tool-specific training; Vanderbilt CAM-ICU clinical implementation terms checked, but confirm permission for any paid-platform redistribution or adaptation
Unit delirium and agitation protocol and medicine policy
gaps: No published clinical scenario may exist until the review phase: this is a specification only.
The branching content, consequences and scoring are the author's reading of the cited sources and have had no clinical review.
Vanderbilt CAM-ICU clinical-use terms and training resources identified; exact tool items and scoring not reproduced. Other uses require contacting CIBS; ICDSC terms remain unresolved.
Doses, routes and durations of any medicine are deliberately absent; NICE places medicine use after failed de-escalation and with prescriber and MHRA safety considerations.
NICE CG103 covers hospital and long-term care in the UK; critical-care-specific sedation and pain management were not read.

2025 SCCM PADIS focused update recommendation webpages have been reviewed but not full evidence tables or validated CAM-ICU/ICDSC tool instructions; antipsychotic evidence is inconclusive and clinician-specific decisions remain necessary.

NICE: Notice of rights not read; paraphrase only.
S-SCCM-PADIS is RED, cite-only; no copyrighted tool questions, figures, scoring rules or guideline tables reproduced.
setting: A fictional adult on a fictional critical care unit.

steps.info: During the night shift, an adult who was calm yesterday becomes restless, pulls at tubing and has fluctuating attention. Arousal and physiological status have not yet been reassessed. A colleague describes the patient as difficult, but this is a new change from baseline.
steps.prompt: What should the nurse prioritize before attributing the change to delirium or choosing a screening tool?

options.text: Stay, protect safety, assess airway, breathing, oxygenation, pain and new physiological or neurological changes; seek urgent review and arrange trained delirium screening when the patient's arousal permits.
options.feedback: A new mental-status or behaviour change is not automatically delirium. The nursing response first assesses acute threats and potentially reversible contributors, protects lines and the patient, and escalates promptly when deterioration is possible. Trained staff use the unit-approved CAM-ICU or ICDSC protocol at an assessable level of arousal; the responsible clinician evaluates the diagnosis. Arousal influences delirium screening. If deep sedation or another limitation prevents a valid screen, record that it is not assessable and why, rather than recording a negative result; reassess eligibility according to the tool and clinical plan.
options.consequence: Immediate safety and physiological assessment may identify a reversible cause and establish whether a delirium screen is assessable.

options.text: Attribute the change to the patient's personality, settle the patient with a sedative from ward stock and plan a screening assessment once the patient is calmer, without first assessing possible acute deterioration.
options.feedback: A recent change needs assessing, not labelling; medicines are prescribed, and NICE places them after de-escalation has failed.
options.consequence: Labelling the behaviour or giving an unauthorized sedative could obscure acute deterioration.

options.text: Document the pulling at tubing and fluctuating attention in the handover notes, maintain routine observations and wait for the next shift to reassess rather than reviewing the new change now.
options.feedback: NICE says to assess promptly once changes are noticed.
options.consequence: Waiting until the next shift could delay identification of an underlying illness or safety threat.

steps.info: At the next shared checkpoint, the treating clinician has diagnosed delirium after assessment. The patient is frightened and attempting to climb out of bed. Family can be contacted by phone; sensory needs and discomfort still require review.
steps.prompt: How can the nurse reduce immediate distress and injury risk without assuming medication is routinely indicated?

observations.label: Behaviour
observations.value: Distressed, trying to get out of bed

observations.label: Immediate safety
observations.value: Risk of falling or dislodging tubing

options.text: Stay, reorient calmly, de-escalate, review pain and needs, involve family or sensory aids as appropriate and urgently escalate persistent danger. Sedation requires authorised assessment and orders.
options.feedback: NICE advocates reorientation and de-escalation, but the SCCM 2025 ICU focused update could not recommend for or against antipsychotics over usual care for established ICU delirium. This is uncertainty, not a routine instruction to use or avoid a specific agent. Harmful behaviour, pain or medical instability require urgent assessment; drug selection and ECG/QT risk are clinician/pharmacy decisions. SCCM 2025 conditionally favors dexmedetomidine over propofol in mechanically ventilated adults when light sedation or reducing delirium is a leading goal. This is not a recommendation to administer dexmedetomidine to every agitated patient or to treat delirium routinely with a sedative; individual sedation goals and hemodynamics matter.
options.consequence: Calm communication, individualised non-drug measures and urgent escalation of persistent danger may support safer care.

options.text: Give haloperidol from ward stock when the patient becomes distressed, expecting the medication to settle the behaviour before reviewing pain, sensory needs or the need for a clinician-directed treatment plan.
options.feedback: Do not administer an antipsychotic without a qualified assessment and order. SCCM's 2025 adult ICU review found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against antipsychotics as routine delirium treatment; the product label includes important ECG/QT and other safety risks. Immediate danger still needs an urgent team response.
options.consequence: Unordered antipsychotic administration could expose the patient to avoidable adverse effects without addressing the cause.

options.text: Reduce stimulation by leaving the frightened patient alone, ask family to wait until the agitation settles and return to reassess later rather than providing reassurance or urgently escalating persistent danger.
options.feedback: Staying away leaves the patient frightened and at risk; NICE advises communication, reorientation and reassurance.
options.consequence: Leaving the patient alone could increase distress and the risk of injury.

steps.info: At the final shared checkpoint, visible agitation has settled and the team is investigating the cause. The patient is quieter than earlier; a clock and calendar are not visible, and several different staff have cared for the patient. Recovery of attention and arousal has not been established.
steps.prompt: Which ongoing care and reassessment distinguish reduced agitation from actual recovery?

observations.label: Environment
observations.value: Clock and calendar not yet visible

observations.label: Care team
observations.value: Several different staff in recent shifts

options.text: Continue team-led reorientation, sleep protection, pain review, sensory aids, safe mobility and family involvement. Monitor hypoactive delirium, document arousal and screen eligibility; report deterioration.
options.feedback: Non-drug care and reassessment continue even after visible agitation settles; a calm or withdrawn patient can still have delirium or another acute problem. The SCCM 2025 update conditionally favors enhanced rehabilitation over usual care but does not specify a bedside dose or universal schedule, so mobility requires individualized team safety checks. Document the actual screen result, arousal level and any reason the tool could not be used. Reassess when the patient becomes assessable.
options.consequence: Continued individualised care and assessment may reveal persistent hypoactive delirium or other neurological change.

options.text: Stop reorientation and other non-drug measures now that the visible agitation has settled, record the patient as recovered and return to routine observation without reassessing attention, arousal or screening eligibility.
options.feedback: NICE recommends communication and reorientation as part of managing delirium.
options.consequence: Stopping reorientation could remove helpful support while disorientation persists.

options.text: Move the patient to a quieter unfamiliar room and change the care team to minimise disturbance, without establishing a clinical need for transfer or maintaining the existing reorientation and reassessment plan.
options.feedback: NICE advises avoiding moving people unless absolutely necessary and keeping a familiar team.
options.consequence: An unnecessary move could worsen disorientation and disrupt continuity of care.

learning_points: New agitation or withdrawal can reflect delirium, pain, oxygenation problems, medication effects or other acute deterioration: assess and urgently escalate possible threats first.
Use an authorised ICU delirium screen only when appropriate and by trained staff; final clinical diagnosis and sedative decisions are not made by an unvalidated case score.
Reorientation, sleep protection, sensory support, family participation and individualized safe mobility are non-drug measures that require ongoing reassessment.
SCCM's 2025 focused update could not recommend for or against antipsychotics over usual care in adult ICU delirium; no routine haloperidol instruction follows from a positive screen.
A patient who cannot undergo a valid delirium assessment must not be recorded as screen-negative. Record the reason and reassess eligibility.
